chapters.title: Chemistry, other sciences and decisions in society
objectives: Distinguish major branches of chemistry using concrete questions.
Explain links between chemistry, health, farming and other disciplines.
Evaluate a chemical technology using evidence about benefits and costs.
paragraphs: Chemistry investigates what substances contain, how their particles are arranged, the properties they show and how they change into other substances. A chemist may identify a powder, measure the amount of a dissolved substance or design a material with a useful property. Observation comes before explanation: “a colourless gas formed” records evidence, while “carbon dioxide formed” is an identification that needs a suitable test. Reliable chemical work combines practical observations with models and numerical measurements.

Branches describe overlapping kinds of questions. Analytical chemistry identifies substances and measures their amounts; testing drinking water for dissolved contaminants is an example. Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, including fuels and many medicines. Inorganic chemistry includes metals, minerals and many salts. Physical chemistry relates changes and properties to energy, rates and particle behaviour. Biochemistry studies chemical processes in living things, such as enzymes breaking down food. A single project may use several branches, so a branch name is a useful focus rather than a barrier.

Chemistry connects sciences through shared problems. A farmer investigating poor crop growth may combine soil chemistry, plant biology and measurements of rainfall. A pharmacist needs chemical knowledge of a medicine and biological knowledge of its effects. Physics helps explain the electricity used in electrolysis and the energy transferred during heating. Mathematics supports concentration calculations and comparisons between samples. Engineering turns a small laboratory process into controlled production, while geography helps explain where raw materials and water are available.

Chemical technologies can improve health, food supply and living conditions. Water-treatment chemicals help reduce disease when used correctly; fertilisers replace nutrients removed by harvests; alloys and polymers provide useful construction materials. Evaluation must consider the whole process: raw-material extraction, manufacturing energy, product use and disposal. Excess fertiliser entering water can encourage excessive algal growth. A useful decision therefore identifies the need, compares workable alternatives and checks evidence about benefits and unwanted effects instead of assuming that every chemical product is either harmless or harmful.
examples: A water supplier asks two questions: “Which dissolved substances are present?” and “How much is present?” Both are analytical chemistry questions. Deciding how a disinfectant affects microbes also brings in biology.

A plant makes steel cooking pots. Investigating how a changed alloy composition affects corrosion links inorganic chemistry to materials engineering. Measuring masses and comparing service lifetimes provides evidence for the decision.

A village compares two fertiliser practices. Practice A gives 300 kg of extra crop and practice B gives 270 kg, but B uses half as much fertiliser. Yield alone favours A; deciding overall value also requires cost, soil and water evidence. The numbers do not establish that either practice is best in every field.

chapters.title: Recognising physical and chemical changes
objectives: Use substance identity to distinguish physical and chemical changes.
Assess observations as evidence rather than automatic proof of reaction.
Explain why compounds can differ from their starting elements.
paragraphs: A physical change alters a state, shape, size or distribution without producing a different chemical substance. Cutting copper wire changes its length but leaves copper. Melting pure ice gives liquid water, so the particles have a different arrangement and movement while retaining their chemical identity. Dissolving can also be physical: when ordinary salt dissolves in water, its ions spread through the water and salt can be recovered by removing the water. This example does not mean that every process involving a liquid is a physical change.

A chemical change forms one or more different substances. When iron rusts in suitable conditions, iron-containing substances with different properties develop. When a fuel burns completely in enough oxygen, new products form; the atoms have been rearranged rather than destroyed. “Easy to reverse” is only a useful clue, not a definition. A broken glass is difficult to restore but breaking is physical. Some chemical reactions can be reversed by a different reaction, so reversibility alone cannot settle the classification.

Colour change, gas formation, a new solid and energy transfer can suggest a chemical reaction, but each observation needs context. Bubbles in boiling water are water vapour, whereas gas from a carbonate reacting with acid is a reaction product. A solid forming when a hot salt solution cools may be unchanged salt crystallising; a solid appearing when two solutions react may be a new insoluble compound. Compare starting materials and products, and use appropriate tests rather than relying on one visible sign.

Compounds may behave very differently from their elements because atoms are joined in new structures and ratios. Metallic iron and yellow sulfur are separate substances in an unreacted mixture; after a suitable teacher-led reaction they form iron sulfide with different properties. This comparison needs controlled preparation and is not an invitation to heat unknown mixtures. Chemical reactions conserve atoms. In a closed system the total mass is conserved, but an open container may appear to lose mass if gas escapes or gain mass if oxygen enters from the air.
examples: Wax first melts near a candle flame: this is physical because wax remains wax. Wax vapour then burns and makes other substances: this is chemical. A single everyday event can include both kinds of change.
A beaker of water bubbles when heated. Cooling the collected vapour returns liquid water, supporting a state-change explanation. Bubbles alone did not prove a new gas substance had been made.

A closed reaction vessel has mass 145.6 g before mixing and 145.6 g afterward. A gas forms inside it, but all material stays in the vessel. Gas formation and unchanged total mass are compatible because atoms have rearranged without leaving the system.

glossary.definition: A change that preserves the chemical identities of the substances involved.
A change producing different substances through rearrangement of atoms.
A substance formed in a chemical reaction.
A system that does not exchange matter with its surroundings.

chapters.title: Investigating heating, cooling and changes of state
objectives: Plan a supervised investigation of a state change.
Read heating and cooling records with correct units.
Explain plateaus and distinguish boiling from evaporation.
paragraphs: A heating record relates temperature to time while energy is transferred to a substance. Before collecting data, identify the material, the amount used, the heating method and the measuring interval. A fair comparison between two samples keeps these conditions similar. A thermometer measures its own temperature after approaching thermal equilibrium with its surroundings, so placement matters: the bulb should be in the sample as instructed, without touching the vessel wall or base. Read the scale at eye level and record units.

For a pure substance at constant pressure, melting or boiling can occur while the temperature stays approximately constant even though heating continues. The transferred energy changes the arrangement and separation of particles rather than increasing their average motion. On an ideal heating graph, these intervals appear as plateaus. Real school graphs may be less flat because of impurities, heat loss, uneven heating or measurement limits. A temperature plateau supports an explanation only alongside observations of the state change.

Cooling reverses energy transfer. A liquid may cool, freeze over a nearly steady-temperature interval and then cool further as a solid. The particles do not disappear when a liquid evaporates or a vapour condenses. Evaporation occurs at the liquid surface at temperatures below boiling as some particles escape; boiling produces vapour throughout the liquid at the boiling temperature for the prevailing pressure. Condensation on a cool surface provides evidence that water vapour is present even when the vapour itself cannot be seen.

Practical state-change work needs teacher supervision, stable apparatus and protection against hot surfaces and splashes. Use the school-approved heating arrangement; never heat a sealed container. Steam and hot water can burn even when no flame is visible. Record observations separately from temperature readings: “solid and liquid both present” is more informative than writing only “melting happened”. Repeat measurements where feasible, plot time on the horizontal axis, and explain limitations rather than adjusting unexpected data to match a textbook graph.
examples: A sample reads 22, 31 and 40 °C at 0, 1 and 2 minutes. From 0 to 2 minutes the mean temperature rise is (40 − 22)/2 = 9 °C per minute. This average need not describe every instant.

A pure sample rises to 64 °C, stays near 64 °C while solid and liquid coexist, then rises again after all solid disappears. The likely melting temperature under those conditions is about 64 °C; the plateau does not mean heating stopped.

Water on the outside of a cold closed bottle is not evidence that water passed through the glass. Water vapour in surrounding air loses energy at the cold surface and condenses. Drying the bottle first and comparing a room-temperature bottle helps test this explanation.

chapters.title: Valency, oxidation states and naming compounds
objectives: Write neutral ionic formulae from ion charges.
Name binary compounds and distinguish valency from oxidation state.
Use brackets correctly for repeated polyatomic ions.
paragraphs: A chemical name and formula describe composition precisely. For a binary compound, only two different elements are present, although there may be more than two atoms. Magnesium oxide contains magnesium and oxygen; magnesium hydroxide contains three elements and is therefore not binary. In common binary ionic names, name the positive ion first and change the non-metal ending to -ide: calcium chloride, aluminium oxide and sodium sulfide. Accurate spelling distinguishes sulfide, which contains sulfur without oxygen, from sulfate, a different ion containing sulfur and oxygen.

Valency describes combining capacity and is commonly written without a sign. Oxidation state is a formal electron-accounting number written with a positive or negative sign. In introductory ionic compounds it often matches the monatomic ion charge: sodium is +1 and oxide oxygen is −2. The sum of oxidation states is zero in a neutral compound. An element in its uncombined form has oxidation state zero. These rules are useful bookkeeping; they do not mean every compound contains separate ions or that a covalent atom has a whole electrical charge.

Some metals form more than one positive ion. The Roman numeral in iron(II) chloride identifies iron in oxidation state +2, while iron(III) chloride identifies +3. It does not count the number of iron atoms. Chloride has charge −1, so charge balance gives FeCl₂ and FeCl₃ respectively. Use the smallest whole-number ratio that makes the total positive and negative charges cancel. The same reasoning gives Mg₃N₂ from Mg²⁺ and N³⁻; writing subscripts mechanically without checking charges can produce an incorrect formula.

A polyatomic ion is a bonded group of atoms with an overall charge; some school texts call it a radical. Examples include hydroxide OH⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, sulfate SO₄²⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻ and ammonium NH₄⁺. Keep the internal formula intact when combining ions. Calcium nitrate requires two nitrate ions to balance Ca²⁺, giving Ca(NO₃)₂. Brackets mean that the subscript multiplies every atom inside, so it contains two nitrogen and six oxygen atoms per formula unit. Ammonium is a positive polyatomic ion, showing that positive ions need not be metals.
examples: For aluminium sulfide, combine Al³⁺ and S²⁻. Two aluminium ions give +6 and three sulfide ions give −6, so the formula is Al₂S₃. The subscripts express a ratio, not the ion charges themselves.
For CuO, oxide contributes −2. The copper must contribute +2 to make zero overall, so the name is copper(II) oxide. Cu₂O instead requires two +1 copper ions and is copper(I) oxide.
For ammonium sulfate, two NH₄⁺ ions balance one SO₄²⁻ ion, giving (NH₄)₂SO₄. Count atoms: N = 2, H = 8, S = 1, O = 4. Omitting the brackets would change the meaning of the formula.

glossary.definition: A compound containing exactly two different elements.
The combining capacity of an atom or group.

chapters.title: Calculating empirical and molecular formulae
objectives: Convert masses to relative amounts of atoms.
Derive empirical formulae from mass and percentage data.
Use relative molecular mass to obtain a molecular formula.
paragraphs: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of the different elements in a compound. A molecular formula gives the actual number of each kind of atom in a molecule. Ethene has molecular formula C₂H₄ and empirical formula CH₂. Water has both empirical and molecular formula H₂O because its ratio is already simplest. Ionic solids are usually represented by formula-unit ratios rather than molecular formulae, since an ionic lattice is not made from separate molecules.

Masses cannot be used directly as atom ratios because different atoms have different masses. Divide each elemental mass by the corresponding relative atomic mass to obtain proportional amounts of atoms. Then divide all these results by the smallest result. If the ratios are close to whole numbers within the precision of the data, use those integers as subscripts. Record your intermediate values so that a mistake can be located. Unless specified otherwise, the examples here use H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16 and Mg = 24.

Percentage-composition problems can be treated as a hypothetical 100 g sample: 40.0% carbon becomes 40.0 g carbon. The procedure is then the same as for masses. A ratio such as 1:1.5 should not be rounded to 1:2. Multiply every ratio by 2 to obtain 2:3; similarly, thirds may require multiplication by 3. The final ratio must be consistent with the accuracy of the data, not forced to a convenient formula. If percentages do not total approximately 100%, check whether an element or other information is missing.

To obtain a molecular formula, first calculate the relative formula mass of the empirical unit by adding its relative atomic masses. Divide the supplied relative molecular mass by that empirical formula mass. The result should be a positive whole-number multiplier, allowing for rounding. Multiply every empirical subscript by the same factor. This extra information is essential: composition alone cannot distinguish CH₂O, C₂H₄O₂ and C₆H₁₂O₆ because all have the same simplest atomic ratio.
examples: A compound contains 12 g carbon and 4 g hydrogen. Relative amounts are 12/12 = 1 and 4/1 = 4. The ratio is 1:4, so its empirical formula is CH₄. Using the mass ratio 3:1 would have given the wrong answer.
A sample contains 2.4 g magnesium and 1.6 g oxygen. Relative amounts are 2.4/24 = 0.10 and 1.6/16 = 0.10. Dividing by 0.10 gives 1:1, hence MgO.

A compound is 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O. For 100 g, relative amounts are about 3.33, 6.7 and 3.33, giving about 1:2:1 and CH₂O. Its empirical mass is 30. If its relative molecular mass is 180, the multiplier is 180/30 = 6, giving C₆H₁₂O₆.

chapters.title: Acids, bases, salts and useful reactions
objectives: Distinguish acids, bases and alkalis using aqueous behaviour.
Predict products of common acid reactions.
Choose safe salt-preparation and neutralisation applications.
paragraphs: In introductory aqueous chemistry, an acid produces hydrogen ions in water and a base neutralises an acid. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water and produces hydroxide ions. All alkalis are bases, but insoluble copper(II) oxide is a base without being an alkali. The pH scale indicates acidity and alkalinity: at ordinary classroom temperature, solutions below pH 7 are acidic, pH 7 is neutral and above pH 7 are alkaline. “Strong” describes the extent of ionisation, while “concentrated” describes the amount dissolved per volume; these words are not interchangeable.

Neutralisation commonly involves acid reacting with base to form a salt and water. A salt contains the positive ion from a base or metal and the negative ion associated with the acid. Hydrochloric acid forms chlorides, sulfuric acid sulfates and nitric acid nitrates. For example, hydrochloric acid plus sodium hydroxide gives sodium chloride and water. Neutralisation can release heat. It is not safe to improvise mixing concentrated acids and alkalis: laboratory work uses approved concentrations, eye protection and teacher supervision.

Acids also react with many carbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide. A suitable test for carbon dioxide is that it turns limewater milky under the prescribed school procedure. Many reactive metals produce a salt and hydrogen with suitable dilute acids, but not every metal reacts this way. Copper does not release hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid under ordinary school conditions. Hydrogen is flammable, so gas tests and metal–acid reactions require supervised small-scale procedures and ignition control.

Salt preparation depends on reactant solubility. A teacher may prepare a soluble salt from an acid and an insoluble base by adding excess base, filtering off what remains and concentrating the solution to crystallise the salt. If both reactants are soluble, controlled titration is needed to find neutralising amounts without leaving excess acid or alkali; these methods are not interchangeable. Everyday applications include suitable treatment of acidic soils and the use of approved antacid medicines. These applications require appropriate quantities and context: a classroom equation alone cannot set an agricultural or medical dose.
examples: Hydrochloric acid and magnesium oxide form magnesium chloride and water: MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O. Counting atoms gives Mg 1, O 1, H 2 and Cl 2 on each side.
Calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. The carbonate pattern predicts the gas; an appropriate test is needed to confirm its identity.

To obtain copper(II) sulfate crystals, a teacher can add excess copper(II) oxide to warm dilute sulfuric acid, filter away unreacted oxide and crystallise the filtrate. Filtering removes excess solid base, but it could not remove dissolved excess sodium hydroxide in an alternative mixture.

chapters.title: Explaining patterns across periods and down groups
objectives: Locate first-twenty elements using electron arrangements.
Explain selected group and period trends with particle ideas.
State limits of introductory periodic trends.
paragraphs: The periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number, so its patterns connect to proton and electron numbers. For the first twenty elements, the number of occupied electron shells gives the period. In the main groups, outer-electron counts connect to group membership: one outer electron for group 1, two for group 2, then three to eight for groups 13 to 18. Helium has two electrons in its only shell and is placed with the noble gases because that shell is full. State the numbering convention because some older tables label the main groups differently.

Across period 3, atomic number increases while electrons are added to the same main shell. Increasing positive nuclear charge generally attracts these electrons more strongly, so atomic radius generally decreases from sodium towards chlorine. Metallic character declines across the period: sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metals, silicon is commonly described as a metalloid, and phosphorus, sulfur and chlorine are non-metals. Not every physical property varies smoothly: melting points depend on structure and bonding, so they do not simply rise or fall across the whole period.

Down a group, additional occupied shells make atoms generally larger. Outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons. Group 1 elements readily lose one outer electron; this becomes easier down the group, so their reactions with water generally become more vigorous. These reactions are demonstrations for a trained teacher, not learner experiments. Group 17 halogens react by gaining an electron in many reactions; their reactivity generally decreases down the group because attraction for an incoming electron is less effective farther from the nucleus.

Chemical patterns support predictions when the kind of reaction is specified. Group 1 metals form +1 ions, group 2 metals form +2 ions, and halogens commonly form −1 ions. Noble gases are much less reactive in ordinary conditions because their outer shell is full, though “unreactive” should not be interpreted as impossible to react under all conditions. A trend is a general relationship drawn from evidence. Distinguish a structural explanation from an observation, and do not extend the first-twenty shell model to all elements without further rules.
examples: An atom has arrangement 2,8,2. It has three occupied shells, placing it in period 3, and two outer electrons, placing it in group 2. Its 12 electrons identify the neutral atom as magnesium.

Compare lithium, 2,1, with sodium, 2,8,1. Both have one outer electron, but sodium has an additional occupied shell. Its outer electron is farther out and more shielded, helping explain its greater reactivity with water.
An atom with 2,8,7 is in period 3 and group 17. Gaining one electron gives a full outer shell and a −1 ion. With Mg²⁺, two such chloride ions are needed, so magnesium chloride is MgCl₂.

chapters.title: Preparing and evaluating local acid–base indicators
objectives: Plan preparation of a plant-pigment indicator under supervision.
Use reference samples and controls to interpret colour changes.
Report limitations of a natural indicator.
paragraphs: An acid–base indicator is a substance whose colour changes over a particular pH range. Some leaves, flowers and fruit skins contain pigments that can serve as indicators, but not every coloured extract responds usefully to pH. A locally available purple leaf or flower can be investigated with teacher approval. Identify the plant reliably and avoid unknown, poisonous or irritating material. A plant extract is a laboratory reagent after preparation; it must not be tasted even if the original plant is normally eaten.

For a school preparation, wash the approved plant material, break it into small pieces and extract the pigment using a small measured volume of warm water under teacher direction. Filter to obtain a clearer coloured solution. Record the plant part, mass or approximate amount, solvent volume and extraction time, because changing these can change colour strength. Water extraction avoids introducing a flammable solvent, though heating and glassware still require supervision. Label the extract and prepare it freshly if storage causes fading or contamination.

Calibrate before testing unknowns. Add the same volume of indicator to equal volumes of a known dilute acidic reference, water and a known dilute alkaline reference supplied by the teacher. Record observed colours rather than assuming universal names: a given extract might be red in acid and green in alkali, but another plant may behave differently. A water sample establishes a comparison near neutral conditions, and a sample without indicator helps reveal the liquid’s own colour. Use clean droppers so that one sample does not contaminate another.

Test approved local samples in separate labelled containers and compare their colours with the references. A matching colour supports a broad classification such as acidic or alkaline; it does not give an exact pH without further calibration. Strongly coloured or cloudy samples can mask an indicator. Adding too much extract can also alter the test mixture or obscure differences. Never mix household cleaners, test unknown chemicals or infer drinking safety from indicator colour. Report ambiguous observations honestly and suggest a pH meter or a suitable standard indicator as a follow-up.
examples: A purple extract turns pink in an approved acidic reference, purple in water and green in an alkaline reference. An uncoloured sample turns pink after the same indicator volume is added. It is reasonable to classify it as acidic within the tested range, but not to assign pH 2 from colour alone.

Tube A contains 5 mL of reference acid and 1 mL of extract; tube B contains 5 mL of an unknown and 5 mL of extract. Their colours are not a fair comparison because the indicator proportion differs. Repeat using equal sample and indicator volumes.

A dark brown drink still looks brown after indicator is added. This is inconclusive, not evidence of neutrality. Compare with a no-indicator sample and use a different suitable measurement method if the original colour masks the response.

chapters.title: Observation, measurement and biological reports
objectives: Distinguish observations from explanations in biology.
Measure biological quantities with suitable units and sampling.
Prepare a clear report containing evidence and limitations.
paragraphs: Biology studies living organisms and their processes. Its branches include botany for plants, zoology for animals, microbiology for microscopic organisms and ecology for relationships with surroundings. These connect to chemistry through substances and reactions in cells, to physics through light and movement, and to mathematics through measurement and data analysis. Scientific terms make descriptions precise: an organism is an individual living thing, a tissue is a group of cooperating similar specialised cells, and a habitat is the place where an organism lives.

Observation records what is detected with the senses or suitable instruments; an inference proposes what it means. “The seedling leans towards the window” is an observation, while “unequal light caused its growth direction” is an explanation to test. Use counts, drawings and measurements instead of vague words where possible. Length may be measured in millimetres or centimetres, mass in grams, and temperature in degrees Celsius. Start a ruler at its zero mark, read scales consistently and report a precision supported by the instrument rather than inventing extra decimal places.

A biological investigation begins with a focused question and a testable prediction. Identify the independent variable to change, the dependent variable to measure and important conditions to control. Living samples vary, so use multiple organisms where appropriate and record a range or mean rather than treating one individual as typical. Repeated readings of the same plant can check measurement consistency, but they are not the same as testing several independent plants. Obtain permission for specimen collection, avoid damaging habitats and follow supervised handling rules for slides and biological material.

A useful report contains a title or question, purpose, prediction, materials, method, results, interpretation, conclusion and limitations. A results table gives labelled quantities and units; the discussion explains patterns without rewriting every number. A drawing from a microscope records structures actually observed, with clear outlines and labelled lines. In the conclusion, answer the original question using the evidence, then state how measurement limits, sample size or uncontrolled conditions affect confidence. A claim that no effect was detected is different from proving that an effect can never occur.
examples: Five seedling lengths are 4, 5, 5, 6 and 10 cm. Their mean is (4 + 5 + 5 + 6 + 10)/5 = 6 cm, while the range is 4–10 cm. Reporting both shows that the mean does not describe every plant.

A learner sees rectangular cell outlines in a leaf slide. The drawing should include these observed outlines, not add a clearly visible nucleus to every cell if nuclei were not resolved. A textbook expectation guides questions but cannot replace observation.

Two pots differ in both watering and light. Their growth difference cannot be attributed confidently to water alone because light is a confounding variable. A stronger design varies watering while keeping light, plant type and starting size comparable.

chapters.title: Testing photosynthesis requirements and reporting evidence
objectives: Interpret controlled experiments on light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll.
Explain destarching and the starch test as indirect evidence.
Recognise confounding variables and limits of leaf investigations.
paragraphs: Photosynthesis makes organic food using light energy, carbon dioxide and water in chlorophyll-containing cells. A school starch investigation does not measure every step directly: it tests whether starch accumulated in a leaf under the investigated conditions. Before comparing treatments, a teacher may destarch suitable plants by keeping them in darkness for a prescribed period. Stored starch is used during respiration, reducing the chance that an earlier store will be mistaken for starch made during the experiment. Plant health and the species used affect how well this preparation works.

To investigate light, a teacher covers part of a leaf with an opaque material while leaving another part exposed and then places the plant in suitable light. The covered and exposed areas share much of the same leaf environment. After the approved exposure, both areas undergo the same supervised starch test. If the exposed region stains blue-black with iodine while the covered region does not, the result supports the need for light for starch accumulation in those conditions. The cover should exclude light without crushing the leaf; a damaged or overheated region creates an alternative explanation.

A variegated leaf has green and non-green regions that can be mapped before testing. Comparing their starch results can support the role of chlorophyll, provided the plant was prepared appropriately and the original colour map is retained. Carbon-dioxide investigations require a comparison between otherwise similar plants with and without an effective carbon-dioxide supply. Any absorbent chemicals and sealed chambers are managed by the teacher. Temperature, water availability, plant type and exposure duration should remain comparable; a hot sealed chamber would introduce a confounding stress.

In the starch test, a teacher first treats the leaf with hot water, removes chlorophyll using ethanol heated indirectly in a water bath, rinses the leaf as instructed and applies iodine solution. Removing green pigment makes the final colour easier to see. Ethanol is flammable and must not be heated directly over a flame. Students working independently should interpret supplied observations or prepare reports rather than perform this procedure alone. A conclusion must match the result: absence of detectable starch may reflect insufficient photosynthesis, preparation problems or rapid use of sugars, not proof that the plant never photosynthesises.
examples: A destarched leaf is half covered and exposed to light. The exposed half becomes blue-black with iodine and the covered half remains yellow-brown. Since light access differs while much of the leaf is shared, the results support light being required for starch accumulation.

Before testing a variegated leaf, a learner draws the green areas. After decolourisation and iodine, blue-black regions align with that map. This correspondence supports chlorophyll’s role; without the original map the learner could not reliably compare green and non-green tissue.

Both a carbon-dioxide-deprived plant and its control fail to show starch. The treatment effect cannot be established because the control did not demonstrate starch accumulation. Check light, preparation, leaf health and test procedure before attributing the result to carbon dioxide.

chapters.title: Ruminant digestion and microbial partnerships
objectives: Trace food through the four compartments of a ruminant stomach.
Explain rumination and microbial cellulose digestion.
Compare ruminant and human digestion without confusing absorption with egestion.
paragraphs: A ruminant such as a cow, goat or sheep feeds on plant material containing much cellulose in cell walls. Mammals do not produce their own cellulase enzymes in sufficient form to digest this cellulose directly. Ruminants gain access to its energy through a partnership with microorganisms in a specialised digestive system. Their stomach has four compartments called the rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum; this is one multi-compartment stomach rather than four independent stomachs. Teeth, jaws, saliva and gut movements also contribute to processing the food.

After initial chewing and swallowing, food enters the fore-stomach compartments, especially the rumen and reticulum. The rumen provides a warm, moist environment where microbes ferment plant material without free oxygen. They produce substances, including volatile fatty acids, that can be absorbed and used by the animal. The microbes obtain habitat and food in return. Gas is also produced during fermentation and normally leaves by eructation. This explanation concerns normal digestion and should not be used to diagnose or treat an animal with abdominal swelling.

Rumination returns a portion of partly processed food, called cud, to the mouth. The animal chews it again and swallows it, reducing particle size and exposing more surface for microbial action. Material subsequently passes through the omasum, where further handling and absorption of water and some dissolved substances occur, to the abomasum, which secretes acid and digestive enzymes. Microbial cells can themselves become a source of nutrients after they pass onward and are digested. Much further digestion and nutrient absorption takes place in the small intestine.

Human and ruminant systems share ingestion, muscular movement, chemical digestion, absorption and egestion, but differ in their treatment of fibrous food. Humans have a single-chambered stomach and cannot obtain energy from grass in the same way as a cow. Dietary fibre still supports normal bowel function in humans. Absorption transfers digested nutrients across the intestinal wall into internal transport systems; egestion expels undigested material as faeces. Excretion instead removes metabolic wastes such as urea, so these processes should not be treated as synonyms.
examples: A cow swallows grass, later brings cud to the mouth and chews again. This second chewing is rumination, not vomiting caused by illness in the normal description. It makes particles smaller and increases access for microbial enzymes.

In a comparison, both a person and a goat eat a cellulose-rich plant. The goat’s fore-stomach microbes ferment much of the cellulose; the human lacks this extensive fore-stomach system. The same plant material therefore need not provide the same usable energy to both.

An arrow sequence for a simplified account is mouth → oesophagus → rumen/reticulum → omasum → abomasum → small intestine → large intestine. A return arrow from rumen/reticulum to mouth represents cud chewing, not a separate route for absorbed nutrients.

chapters.title: Breathing and gaseous exchange in mammals
objectives: Trace air through the respiratory system.
Explain ventilation using volume and pressure changes.
Relate alveolar features to diffusion into and out of blood.
paragraphs: Air enters the mammalian respiratory system through the nose or mouth and passes through the pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and smaller bronchioles to the alveoli. Nasal passages help warm, moisten and filter incoming air. Rings of cartilage help keep the trachea and major bronchi open. Mucus traps many particles and cilia move the mucus towards the throat for removal. These defences reduce exposure of delicate exchange surfaces, but they do not make inhaled smoke or dust harmless.

Ventilation is the bulk movement of air into and out of the lungs. During normal inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens, while external intercostal muscles help raise the ribs. The thoracic volume increases and pressure within the lungs falls slightly below atmospheric pressure, so air moves inward. The lungs expand with the chest through their mechanical connection to the chest wall via the pleural arrangement. They do not actively pull air in by contracting their own muscles.

During quiet expiration the inspiratory muscles relax, the diaphragm returns towards its domed shape and elastic recoil reduces lung volume. Pressure within the lungs rises slightly above atmospheric pressure and air moves out. Forceful expiration can involve additional muscles, so the description of quiet breathing does not cover every breathing situation. Airflow responds to pressure differences. The amount and rate of ventilation can change with activity, but neither a fast breathing rate nor a large breath alone specifies exactly how much oxygen reaches body tissues.

Gaseous exchange occurs mainly across alveolar and capillary walls by diffusion. Oxygen has a higher partial pressure in alveolar air than in arriving blood and moves into the blood; carbon dioxide moves in the opposite direction. Numerous alveoli provide a large area, thin walls give a short diffusion path, moisture allows gases to dissolve, and blood flow plus ventilation maintain the gradients. Ventilation supplies fresh air, gaseous exchange transfers gases across surfaces, and cellular respiration releases usable energy in cells. These related processes should be distinguished.
examples: On inspiration, an increase in chest volume lowers lung air pressure relative to outside air. Air therefore flows down the pressure difference into the lungs. “The lungs suck because oxygen is needed” gives a purpose without the physical mechanism.

A model with two balloons inside a bottle and a rubber sheet at its base can show that moving the sheet down increases enclosed volume and inflates the balloons. Its limitations include a rigid bottle instead of moving ribs and a flat sheet instead of a domed diaphragm.

If the alveolar surface becomes thicker, diffusion has a longer path. Even with air entering the lungs, gas transfer can become less effective. This shows why ventilation and exchange are separate steps; the explanation is educational rather than a diagnosis.

chapters.title: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration: evidence and investigations
objectives: Compare aerobic respiration with anaerobic pathways.
Interpret evidence from living-material and yeast investigations.
Plan controls and explain limitations of respiration measurements.
paragraphs: Cellular respiration is a set of reactions that transfers energy from food into forms cells can use, including ATP. Energy is transferred rather than created. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen; its overall school word equation is glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, with energy transferred. In eukaryotic cells many aerobic stages occur in mitochondria, although the first stage of glucose breakdown occurs in cytoplasm. Living plants respire as well as animals, during both day and night, because their cells continually need energy.

When oxygen supply is insufficient, some cells can obtain a smaller amount of usable energy through anaerobic pathways. In muscle cells, a school-level summary is glucose → lactate, with a smaller energy transfer than in aerobic respiration. Yeast can ferment sugars to ethanol and carbon dioxide when oxygen is unavailable. The products therefore depend on the organism and pathway; it is incorrect to give ethanol as the main anaerobic product of human muscle. Carbon dioxide from yeast can inflate dough, while heat in a warm environment affects both yeast activity and gas behaviour.

An investigation needs an observable response linked to respiration. In a teacher-led comparison, germinating seeds may release more carbon dioxide or warm more than a suitable non-living comparison sample. A control helps distinguish living activity from room-temperature changes or apparatus effects. In a yeast experiment, a known sugar supply, equal yeast quantity and controlled temperature permit comparisons. A gas volume measured over time can indicate gas production, but trapped air, leaks and dissolved gas affect results. A gas test may be needed to support the identity of the collected gas.

Neither bubbling nor carbon dioxide alone proves that respiration was anaerobic. Aerobic respiration can also produce carbon dioxide, and visible bubbles can include expanding trapped air. Oxygen conditions must be controlled and documented by an approved method if comparing aerobic and anaerobic processes. All cultures and chemical gas tests require school guidance; do not culture unknown microbes or seal a fermenting system without pressure relief. In a report, show raw data, calculate rates over stated intervals and explain controls, repeats and limitations before drawing a conclusion about living metabolism.
examples: A yeast mixture gives 24 mL of gas over 6 minutes under the prescribed conditions. Its mean measured rate is 24/6 = 4 mL per minute. This is a gas-production rate, not a direct measurement of total ATP production.

A flask of germinating seeds becomes 2 °C warmer while a matched control changes by 0 °C. This supports energy transfer as heat from living seed activity, provided insulation, starting temperatures and sample amounts were comparable.

Yeast with sugar produces carbon dioxide, but the flask also contains oxygen. The observation supports metabolic gas production but does not establish exclusively anaerobic conditions. A stronger investigation documents oxygen availability and uses appropriate controls.

chapters.title: Gaseous exchange in leaves, stems and roots
objectives: Explain diffusion through stomata and other plant surfaces.
Distinguish respiration, photosynthesis and net gas exchange.
Predict the effects of light and waterlogged soil with stated conditions.
paragraphs: Plants exchange gases with their surroundings without mammalian lungs or a blood system. Gases move mainly by diffusion along concentration or partial-pressure gradients. In many leaves, stomata allow air to pass between outside air and internal air spaces. Thin moist surfaces of mesophyll cells allow gases to dissolve and diffuse into or out of cells. Guard cells regulate stomatal opening, connecting the supply of carbon dioxide for photosynthesis with the need to limit water loss. The pattern of stomata and opening differs among plants and conditions.

Other organs also need gases. Lenticels provide exchange routes in the outer tissues of many woody stems. Young stems and other thin surfaces can exchange gases across their outer layers, while roots obtain oxygen mainly from air spaces in well-aerated soil. Oxygen diffuses through moist root surfaces to respiring cells. Soil that remains waterlogged has much less effective gas supply because diffusion through water is much slower than through air. Root injury in waterlogged soil therefore involves oxygen availability as well as water abundance.

Every living plant cell respires, taking in oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide in aerobic respiration. Photosynthetic cells in sufficient light also take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen through photosynthesis. These processes occur simultaneously in a green leaf during daylight. Net exchange is their combined outcome, not evidence that one has stopped. When photosynthesis exceeds respiration, the leaf shows net carbon-dioxide uptake and oxygen release; in darkness, photosynthesis stops while respiration continues, giving net oxygen uptake and carbon-dioxide release.

At a compensation condition, photosynthetic carbon-dioxide uptake balances respiratory release, so little net carbon-dioxide exchange is detected even though both processes remain active. The balance changes with light, temperature, tissue condition and other limits on photosynthesis. Stomatal closure can reduce carbon-dioxide entry and water loss at the same time. A prediction should therefore state its conditions: bright light may favour net oxygen release in a healthy, adequately watered leaf, but bright light alone does not guarantee it if stomata are closed or another factor is limiting.
examples: A healthy leaf in suitable bright light produces 12 arbitrary units of oxygen by photosynthesis while respiration uses 4 units over the same interval. Net oxygen release is 12 − 4 = 8 units; respiration has not stopped.

At night a green plant continues to respire. With no light-driven photosynthesis, oxygen moves into its living tissues and carbon dioxide moves out overall. The same diffusion principles apply although the net direction differs from a productive daylight leaf.

A pot is kept permanently flooded. Its roots may lack oxygen despite being surrounded by water because air-filled soil spaces are lost and oxygen diffuses slowly through water. Drainage can improve aeration; it is not explained by saying roots need no water.

chapters.title: Investigating food, plant transport and pulse rate
objectives: Interpret nutrient tests with positive and negative controls.
Evaluate plant water-transport investigations and their limitations.
Calculate pulse rate and prepare a clear biological investigation report.
paragraphs: Practical biology connects a question to a measurable response, with controls that test alternative explanations. Food analysis asks whether a detectable nutrient is present in a prepared sample; a plant-transport investigation follows water movement or estimates water uptake; a pulse investigation counts arterial pressure waves over time. These questions use different methods, so one procedure cannot substitute for another. In every case, define the sample, record the method, collect results with units and separate the observed result from the broader conclusion.

Under teacher supervision, iodine solution can indicate starch by a blue-black colour. Benedict’s reagent can indicate reducing sugars after the prescribed water-bath heating, with colour changes that may progress from blue towards green, yellow, orange or brick-red depending on conditions. The biuret test gives a lilac or purple colour in the presence of protein. A teacher-led ethanol emulsion test can indicate lipids by a milky emulsion after the specified mixing with water; ethanol must be kept away from ignition. These chemical tests must not be attempted by tasting samples or reagents, and a negative reducing-sugar test does not establish that every kind of carbohydrate is absent.

For a food test, a positive control contains a known target nutrient and should show the expected response; a negative control, often water, should not. Keep sample volumes, reagent amounts and any heating time comparable. If the positive control fails, a negative unknown cannot be interpreted confidently because the method may have failed. Food colour or cloudiness can mask results, and several nutrients may be present in one food. Detecting protein is not a complete assessment of a food’s nutritional value or its safety.

A teacher-prepared cut stem placed in coloured water can reveal coloured xylem pathways, supporting the location of water transport. It does not directly show sugar movement in phloem. A potometer measures water uptake through a cut shoot and is commonly used as an estimate of transpiration, but uptake is not identical to vapour loss because some water remains in tissues or is used in other processes. The apparatus must be watertight and prepared as instructed to avoid air entering the water column. Keep leaf area, temperature, light and humidity similar when investigating one chosen environmental factor.

A pulse can be counted at the wrist using light pressure with fingers rather than the thumb, whose own pulse can confuse the count. Count for a stated interval and convert to beats per minute if needed. Compare a resting period with gentle ordinary activity only under the school’s inclusive guidance; supplied data are a suitable alternative for anyone unable to participate. Keep posture, counting interval and timing after activity comparable, allow recovery and never use a classroom result as a medical diagnosis. Counting over very short intervals magnifies the effect of a one-beat error.

A report states the question, prediction, method, results, calculations, conclusion and limitations. In a pulse report, give actual counts and counting durations before converted rates. In a plant report, distinguish water uptake from the inferred transpiration rate. In a food report, list controls as well as unknown samples. Repeats and independent samples support reliability, but averaging cannot repair a systematically faulty method. Present data that do not fit the prediction, explain possible causes and recommend a change that directly addresses the identified limitation.
examples: A learner counts 18 pulses in 15 seconds. The converted rate is 18 × (60/15) = 72 beats per minute. A one-beat counting error would change the result by 4 beats per minute, showing why interval choice matters.

An unknown sample stays blue with Benedict’s reagent, but the known glucose control also stays blue after the same treatment. The unknown cannot be confidently classed as lacking reducing sugar because the test procedure or reagent may have failed.

A potometer records 0.8 mL water uptake in 10 minutes, giving 0.08 mL per minute. Calling this the measured uptake rate is accurate. Calling it the exact transpiration rate ignores water retained in tissues and possible apparatus effects.

chapters.title: Reaction types in fuels, food and everyday materials
objectives: Classify combination, decomposition, displacement and combustion reactions.
Connect balanced equations with burning and digestion.
Distinguish reaction type from energy transfer and reaction rate.
paragraphs: Chemical reactions can be grouped by patterns in reactants and products. In combination, two or more reactants form one product; in decomposition, one reactant produces two or more products. In displacement, a more reactive element can replace a less reactive one from a suitable compound. These categories describe patterns rather than visible appearance. A reaction can fit more than one description: magnesium reacting with oxygen is both combination and combustion. Always show the equation or specify the criterion instead of treating the labels as mutually exclusive boxes.

Combustion is reaction with an oxidising agent, commonly oxygen, that transfers energy rapidly and often produces a flame. Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon in enough oxygen forms carbon dioxide and water. Limited oxygen may lead to incomplete combustion, producing carbon monoxide and/or carbon particles as well as other products. Carbon monoxide is colourless and poisonous, so fuel-burning equipment needs proper ventilation and safe operation. A yellow smoky flame can indicate incomplete combustion, but the absence of visible smoke does not prove that combustion gases are harmless.

Digestion connects reaction chemistry to living organisms. Enzymes accelerate the breakdown of large food molecules; many digestive reactions are hydrolysis, in which water participates in breaking bonds. Starch is broken down through smaller carbohydrates to glucose, proteins to smaller peptides and amino acids, and fats to fatty acids and glycerol in a school summary. Digestion is not the same as cellular respiration: digestion prepares absorbable nutrients, while respiration transfers energy from substances such as glucose inside cells. “Food breaks down” is too vague to identify which process is meant.

Reaction pattern, energy transfer and rate answer different questions. An exothermic reaction transfers energy to the surroundings; an endothermic process takes in energy from them. A fast reaction need not release more total energy than a slow one using the same amounts. A catalyst changes the rate of a reaction without being consumed overall, and enzymes are biological catalysts. To compare rates fairly, control quantities, temperature and exposed surface as appropriate. School combustion, displacement and heating investigations require teacher supervision; equations are models for interpreting reactions, not instructions for unsupervised mixing.
examples: For magnesium combustion, 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. There are two Mg atoms and two O atoms on each side. It is combination because the reactants form one product, and combustion because magnesium reacts energetically with oxygen.

For methane combustion, CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Carbon balances at one atom, hydrogen at four and oxygen at four on each side. This equation represents complete combustion and does not describe every product when oxygen is limited.

For displacement in a suitable solution, Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Zinc replaces copper in the compound, while the sulfate group remains unchanged in this overall equation. The equation is balanced with coefficients of one throughout.

workbookQuestions.content: Correct this explanation: “Digestion burns food using oxygen in the stomach, and a faster enzyme always creates more energy.” Include digestion, respiration and rate.
workbookQuestions.answerKey: Digestion uses mechanical processes and enzyme-catalysed reactions to form absorbable molecules; it is not fuel combustion in the stomach. workbookQuestions.content: Using the supplied equation 2C + O₂ → 2CO, count atoms on both sides, identify whether combustion is complete or incomplete, and write a safety implication.
workbookQuestions.answerKey: Each side has two C and two O atoms. It represents incomplete combustion because carbon monoxide forms rather than all carbon becoming carbon dioxide. Fuel equipment needs safe use and appropriate ventilation; never use the equation as a reason to generate carbon monoxide experimentally.
